summary: Describes two reference video traffic models for evaluating RTP congestion control: a statistical model of a live encoder responding to rate requests, and a trace-driven one based on real encoded frame sizes. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8593 describes two fake video sources that stand in for a real live video encoder when testing RTP congestion control. One is built from statistical formulas with adjustable parameters, the other replays frame sizes recorded from a real encoder. Both are meant to be repeatable, so that a test result measures the congestion control algorithm and not the encoder.

questions: video traffic model for congestion control
subtitle: Two ways to fake a live video encoder so that RTP congestion control can be tested repeatably.

tldr.problem: Testing a candidate RTP congestion control algorithm against a real live encoder adds noise, because a real encoder reacts slowly and does not hit its target rate exactly, and the results are hard to repeat.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC presents two reference synthetic video sources: a statistical model whose parameters describe how an encoder lags behind a rate change and fluctuates around the target, and a trace-driven model that reuses frame sizes recorded from a real encoder.
tldr.outcome: Both models are simple to implement and can be combined into a hybrid that uses the statistical model for transients and the trace for steady state, and the RFC recommends testing candidate algorithms with them before wide deployment.

today: RFC 8593 is an Informational document from May 2019 that no RFC obsoletes or updates. It records two reference traffic models for evaluating congestion control candidates, and the RFC recommends testing a candidate algorithm with them before deploying it widely.

sections.title: Why a Synthetic Video Source
sections.content:
When evaluating candidate congestion control algorithms for real-time interactive media, the traffic patterns produced by a live video encoder matter. Unlike synthetic traffic sources, which can conform perfectly to the rate-changing requests of the congestion control module, a live video encoder is often slow to react to such changes, and its output rate typically deviates from the target rate because of uncertainties in the encoder's rate-control process. The end-to-end delay and loss performance of a real-time media flow is then affected by rate variations the encoder introduces.

At the same time, the evaluation of a candidate RTP congestion control algorithm should mostly reflect the performance of the congestion control module and be somewhat decoupled from the peculiarities of any specific video codec. Evaluation tests should also be repeatable and easily duplicated across different candidate algorithms.

The document's answer is to evaluate congestion control algorithms with a synthetic video traffic source model that captures the key characteristics of a live encoder, and that has tunable parameters so it can be adjusted to reflect the wide variation in real-world encoder behavior. Two reference models are presented: one based on statistical modeling, the other driven by frame size and interval traces recorded from a real encoder. The RFC also discusses the advantages and drawbacks of each and how they can be combined into a hybrid model.
sections.plainLanguage: A real video encoder takes time to react when the network says it should slow down, and it never hits the target rate exactly. If you test a congestion control algorithm against a real encoder, the result mixes the algorithm's behaviour with the encoder's quirks and is hard to repeat. The RFC therefore describes a stand-in video source with the same character but under the tester's control.

sections.title: What the Source Must Do, and How It Is Driven
sections.content:
A live video encoder meets a target rate by varying encoding parameters such as the quantization step size, the frame rate and the picture resolution, based on its estimate of the video content. Several factors stop the output rate from matching the target exactly. The output rate typically deviates because of uncertainties in the captured scene. After a significant change in target rate, the output frame sizes sometimes fluctuate for a short transient period before the output rate converges to the new target. And while most frames in a live session are predictive frames, the encoder can occasionally generate a large intra-coded frame, or a frame partly containing intra-coded blocks, to recover from losses, to re-sync with the receiver, or during the transient period of responding to a change in target rate or resolution.

A synthetic video source should therefore be able to change bitrate, which includes changing the frame rate or the spatial resolution or skipping frames on request; fluctuate around the target bitrate specified by the congestion control module; show a delay in converging on the target bitrate; and generate intra-coded or repair frames on demand. Beyond that, the outcome should have low computational complexity, otherwise it defeats the purpose of substituting for a live encoder; temporal pattern similarity, so that individual trace instances mimic the temporal pattern of a real encoder; statistical resemblance, matching the real encoder in mean, variance, peak and autocorrelation coefficients of the bitrate, and holding across time scales from tens of milliseconds to sub-seconds; and a wide range of coverage, so it can be configured to cover a wide range of codec behaviors and content variations.

The model sits inside the sender and generates a sequence of dummy video frames with varying size and interval, which other modules then process to transmit the video stream. It accepts a set of incoming calls. The target bitrate R_v is a request in bits per second; depending on the congestion control algorithm the update requests may be periodic, for example once per second, or made on demand, for instance only when a drastic bandwidth change is observed. The target frame rate FPS is the instantaneous frame rate, which depends on the native camera capture rate and on the target or preferred frame rate configured by the application or user. The target frame resolution XY is the preferred resolution in pixels, governed by the capture resolution, the display size of the destination screen, and the current target bitrate, since a very low resolution does not pair with a very high bitrate. Instant frame skipping asks the source to skip encoding one or several captured frames, for instance when a drastic decrease in available bandwidth is detected. On-demand generation of an intra frame asks for another I-frame to avoid further error propagation at the receiver when severe packet losses are observed; that request usually comes from the error control module and can be started by the sender or by the receiver through Full Intra Request messages.

One outgoing call is the rate range [R_min, R_max], which captures the dynamic rate range the real encoder could produce for the given content. It depends on the content complexity and the display type, so it does not change with R_v but may change over time as the content changes.
sections.plainLanguage: The stand-in source has to do four things that a real encoder does: change its rate on request, wobble around the rate that was asked for, take time to settle on a new rate, and produce a large refresh frame when the test asks for one. It is driven by calls from the congestion control module, the application and the error control module, and it reports back the range of rates it can produce.

sections.title: The Statistical Model
sections.content:
The statistical model reproduces the behaviour of a live encoder with a small set of tunable parameters. The target bitrate request R_v and the target frame rate FPS come from outside. The model adds the encoder reaction latency tau_v, the burst duration K_d of the transient period, the burst frame size K_B, the reference frame interval t0 = 1/FPS, the reference frame size B0 = R_v/8/FPS, the scaling parameters SCALE_t and SCALE_B of the zero-mean Laplacian distributions describing the deviations in normalized frame interval and frame size, and the minimum and maximum rates R_min and R_max supported by the encoder type or content activity.

Reaction to a rate change is time-damped. When the encoder has reacted to a rate-change request at time t, it ignores all later rate-change requests until time t plus tau_v. The output bitrate R_o during the interval from t to t plus tau_v is treated as a transient state, and the reaction to a new target is characterized by high variation in output frame sizes. The model assumes the average output bitrate during the transient matches the target, so the occasional burst of large frames is followed by smaller-than-average encoded frames. The burst is described by its duration K_d, the number of frames in the burst event, and its size K_B, the size of the initial burst frame, which is typically significantly larger than the average steady-state frame size. The same two parameters can be used to mimic the insertion of a large on-demand I-frame after severe packet loss.

At steady state the output bitrate is modeled as fluctuating randomly around the target, as the combination of two random processes: the frame interval t and the output frame size B. For simplicity the deviations of t and B from their reference levels are modeled as independent and identically distributed random variables following the Laplacian distribution. The deviation in the normalized frame interval, DELTA_t = (t-t0)/t0, follows a zero-mean Laplacian distribution with scaling parameter SCALE_t, which sets the width of the distribution and so the amount of fluctuation in the actual frame intervals. The deviation in the normalized frame size, DELTA_B = (B-B0)/B0, follows a second zero-mean Laplacian distribution with scaling parameter SCALE_B. Both values can be obtained by fitting to empirical data from a given encoder. Finally, the output bitrate is clipped to the dynamic range [R_min, R_max], which in reality is dictated by the scene and motion complexity of the content but which the model takes from the application.
sections.plainLanguage: This model is a set of formulas. After the congestion controller asks for a new rate, the model ignores further requests for a fixed reaction time, then produces one oversized frame followed by smaller ones so that the average matches the request. In between requests it wobbles around the target rate, and the size of the wobble is set by two fitted parameters.

sections.title: The Trace-Driven Model
sections.content:
The trace-driven approach runs an actual live video encoder over a set of chosen raw video sequences and uses the encoder's output traces to build a synthetic source. The recorded traces naturally exhibit the temporal fluctuations around a target bitrate that a real encoder produces.

The steps are: choose one or more representative raw video sequences; encode them with a real live encoder, repeating the process for a number of bitrates and keeping only the sequence of frame sizes for each bitrate; build a data structure holding that output, allowing easy bitrate lookup; on a target bitrate request, look up the closest stored bitrates and use their frame-size sequences to approximate the frames to output; and let the synthetic source output encoded frames with dummy contents but realistic sizes.

Choosing the video sequence is a careful step, and for interactive video conferencing the recommendation is a sequence whose content resembles a talking head, for example from a news broadcast or a recording of an actual video conferencing call. The length is a trade-off: too long makes the trace data structures hard to manage, and too short gives an obvious periodic pattern in the output frame sizes that biases the results. It has been empirically determined that a sequence 2 to 4 minutes long avoids the periodic pattern.

The encoder is usually configured with a fixed frame rate and a fixed resolution, for example 30 fps and 720p, so that the rate can be reached by varying the quantization step size. The first frame can be assumed to be an I-frame and the rest P-frames. The range from R_min to R_max is divided into n_s steps, giving an encoding bitrate ladder of n_s + 1 choices equally spaced by the step length l = (R_max - R_min)/n_s. The minimum value of n_s is 1, the maximum depends on the memory available for the map, and a reasonable choice is a step length of 200 kbps. The traces are stored in a map whose keys are bitrates and whose values are vectors of frame sizes.

Using the traces, the codec keeps two variables: r_current, a key of the trace map, and t_current, an index into the frame-size vector stored under that key. When R_v changes, r_current is set to the largest stored bitrate that does not exceed the requested rate, with the requested rate clamped to the range covered by the trace file. When a new frame is due, t_current advances, wrapping around the vector while always skipping the first SkipFrames entries, which avoids the effect of periodically sending a large I-frame followed by several smaller-than-average P-frames. A typical value of SkipFrames is 20, and it could be set to 0 if the effect of sending I-frames periodically is what is being studied.

The frame size is then calculated in one of three ways. When the request lies inside the range covered by the trace file, the size is a linear interpolation between the frame sizes stored under r_current and under r_current + l. When the request is below the trace range, the size is scaled with respect to the lowest bitrate in the trace file, and when it is above the range it is scaled with respect to the highest. The resulting size is clipped between fs_min, for example 10 bytes, and fs_max, for example 1 MB.
sections.plainLanguage: This model records what a real encoder actually produces. A real encoder is run over a few minutes of representative video at a ladder of bitrates, and the size of each frame is kept. At run time the source looks up the recorded sizes closest to the rate the congestion controller asked for and replays them, with the sizes scaled when the request falls outside the recorded range.

sections.title: Combining the Two Models
sections.content:
The two models each have their own advantages and drawbacks, and both are fairly simple to implement. Fitting the parameters of a statistical model to real encoder output takes significantly greater effort than obtaining encoded frame-size data for a trace-driven model. Once validated, however, the statistical model is more flexible at mimicking a wide range of encoder and content behaviors simply by varying its parameters, whereas a trace-driven model relies by definition on extra data collection for each new codec or video content.

In general the trace-driven model is more realistic for mimicking the ongoing steady-state behavior of a video source with fluctuations around a constant target rate, while the statistical model is more versatile for simulating transient behavior, such as when a sudden rate change is encountered. The RFC describes a hybrid model in which the steady-state behavior is driven by traces and the transient-state behavior is driven by the statistical model.

In the hybrid model the traffic source operates in a transient state if the requested target rate R_v is substantially different from the previous target, and in a steady state otherwise. During the transient state a total of K_d frames are generated by the statistical model, giving one big burst frame of size K_B followed by K_d - 1 smaller frames. In the steady state the source generates a frame according to the trace-driven model for the target rate, while modulating the frame interval according to the distribution specified by the statistical model. One example criterion for entering the transient state is whether the rate change exceeds 10% of the previous target rate. Because the transient behavior comes from the statistical model, the hybrid model follows the time-damping mechanism of the statistical model after a substantial rate change, which is governed by tau_v.

The statistical, trace-driven and hybrid models have been implemented as a stand-alone, platform-independent synthetic traffic source module that can be integrated into network simulation platforms such as ns-2 and ns-3, as well as into testbeds using a real network. The stand-alone module is available as an open-source implementation.
sections.plainLanguage: The two models suit different moments. Recorded traces reproduce the normal wobble around a steady rate, while the formulas handle the awkward moments when the rate changes suddenly. The hybrid model uses each where it fits: traces while things are steady, formulas during a change.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The synthetic video traffic models described in the document do not impose any security threats. They are designed to mimic realistic traffic patterns for evaluating candidate RTP-based congestion control algorithms, so as to ensure stable operation of the network.

The RFC states that it is RECOMMENDED that candidate algorithms be tested using the video traffic models it presents before wide deployment over the Internet. It adds that if the generated synthetic traffic flows are sent over the Internet, they also need to be congestion controlled.
sections.plainLanguage: The fake video sources are not a security risk in themselves. The RFC advises testing a congestion control algorithm with them before putting it on the Internet, and warns that generated traffic sent over the Internet still has to be congestion controlled like any other traffic.

items.title: tau_v, reaction latency
items.text: Example value 0.2 s. Further rate requests are ignored for this long.

items.title: K_d and K_B, the burst
items.text: Example values 8 frames and 13.5 KB for 720p at 30 fps with H.264/AVC.

items.title: t0 and B0, the references
items.text: Example values 33 ms and 4.17 KB, where t0 is 1/FPS and B0 is R_v/8/FPS.

items.title: SCALE_t and SCALE_B
items.text: Example values 0.15 each. They set the width of the two Laplacian distributions.

items.title: R_min and R_max
items.text: Example values 150 kbps and 1.5 Mbps, the range the encoder type or content activity supports.
